name: Generac Guardian 22kW
summary: Generac's best-selling air-cooled standby: 22kW on propane, starts itself in an outage, and sized for most 2,000–3,000 sq ft homes with central air.
verdict:
The Guardian 22kW is the default whole-house [standby generator](/glossary/standby-generator/) for a reason: it is big enough for most homes, it starts itself, and it runs as long as the gas holds. If you want outages to be a non-event, this is the size to quote first.

**Size it to your loads.** Generac rates it at 22,000 watts on propane, and its current spec page lists 21,000 watts on natural gas (earlier units were rated 19,500 watts on natural gas). At 240 volts, 21,000 watts is about 87 amps. A 3-ton central air conditioner, a fridge, a well pump and lighting together sit well under that, so most homes can back up the whole panel. Use the [wattage calculator](/tools/generator-wattage-calculator/) if you have electric heat or two AC units.

**Fuel is the real decision.** On natural gas it runs as long as utility pressure holds. On propane, Generac lists 2.53 gallons per hour at half load. A 500-gallon tank filled to 80% holds about 400 gallons, which is roughly 158 hours, about six and a half days, at that load.

**Install and upkeep.** It needs a pad, a permit, a gas fitter, a licensed electrician and an [automatic transfer switch](/glossary/transfer-switch/). The unit weighs 466 lb and uses Generac's 999cc G-Force 1000 engine. Plan on yearly oil, filter and spark plug service.

Owners report that it simply works when the grid drops and like the Mobile Link status alerts; the common complaints are installation cost and dealer wait times. It is the top standby pick in our [home generator for power outages](/best-home-generator-for-power-outages/) guide, and our [Generac generator cost](/generac-generator-cost/) breakdown covers install budgets.

faqs.q: Can the Generac Guardian 22kW run central air?
faqs.a: Yes, in most homes. Generac rates it at 22,000 W on propane and 21,000 W on natural gas, and a typical 3- to 4-ton central air conditioner runs at roughly 3,500 to 5,000 W once started. You can usually run one AC alongside the fridge, well pump and lights. Two AC units or electric heat need a load calculation, and Generac sells load-shedding modules for that case.

faqs.q: How long will the Guardian 22kW run on propane?
faqs.a: Generac lists 2.53 gallons per hour at half load and 3.71 gallons per hour at full load. A 500-gallon tank is filled to about 400 gallons, so that is roughly 158 hours at half load or about 108 hours at full load. On utility natural gas there is no tank limit, only regular oil checks during long runs.

name: Generac GP8000E
summary: An 8,000-watt gasoline portable with electric start and COsense CO shutoff, sized for a well pump, fridge, freezer and furnace through a 30-amp transfer switch.
verdict:
The GP8000E is the portable to buy when you want big gasoline output from a brand with parts and service everywhere. It is our pick for most watts per dollar in the gas class.

**Size it to your loads.** Generac rates it at 8,000 [running watts](/glossary/running-watts/) and 10,000 [starting watts](/glossary/starting-watts/). A 1 HP 240V well pump, a refrigerator, a freezer, a furnace blower and lights fit with room to spare if you let the motors start one at a time. A window AC can replace one of those loads.

**The L14-30 outlet is the point.** The panel has two 20-amp GFCI duplex outlets and a 120/240V 30-amp [L14-30R](/glossary/l14-30/). That outlet feeds a power inlet box and a manual transfer switch such as the [Reliance 31406CRK](/gear/reliance-31406crk/), so 240V loads like a well pump are on the table.

**Runtime and weight.** The 7.9-gallon tank gives about 10 to 11 hours at half load from the 420cc engine, depending on the version. It weighs about 198 lb, so it rolls on its never-flat wheels rather than being carried. COsense shuts the engine down if carbon monoxide builds up around it.

Owners report easy electric starts and solid build; the main complaints are open-frame noise and gasoline use in long outages. It ranks in our [best gas generator](/best-gas-generator/) and [generator for well pump](/best-generator-for-well-pump/) guides.

faqs.q: Can the Generac GP8000E run a well pump?
faqs.a: Yes, most residential pumps. A 1 HP 240V submersible typically needs about 1,000 running watts and several thousand watts to start, and the GP8000E offers 10,000 starting watts through its L14-30R outlet. Feed it into a transfer switch, start the pump first, then add the fridge and freezer. Pumps of 2 HP and up need a closer look at the pump maker's starting figure.

faqs.q: GP8000E vs GP6500: which should you buy?
faqs.a: Buy the GP8000E if you need a 240V well pump plus a fridge, freezer and furnace, since it adds 1,500 running and 1,875 starting watts. Buy the [GP6500](/gear/generac-gp6500/) if your loads stay under about 5,000 watts; it is lighter at about 172 lb, and its 389cc engine stretches the same 7.9-gallon tank to 11.5 hours at half load.

name: DuroMax XP12000EH
summary: A 12,000-watt dual fuel portable with a 50-amp outlet, for buyers who want near-standby output on wheels and can live with the weight, noise and fuel burn.
verdict:
The XP12000EH is about as much generator as you can still roll around. It suits a house with gas heat that wants most of its circuits back through a 50-amp inlet, without paying for a standby install.

**The numbers.** DuroMax rates it at 9,500 running and 12,000 starting watts on gasoline, and 9,025 running and 11,400 starting watts on propane, from a 457cc engine. That is only a 5% loss on propane, better than many [dual fuel](/glossary/dual-fuel/) rivals. At 240 volts, 9,500 watts is about 40 amps.

**The 50-amp outlet is the point.** The panel adds a 120/240V 50-amp 14-50R next to the L14-30R, two GFCI duplexes and a 120V 30-amp twist-lock. Paired with a 50-amp inlet like the [Reliance PBN50](/gear/reliance-pbn50/) and a panel [interlock kit](/glossary/interlock-kit/), it can carry a smaller central AC plus essentials, depending on the AC's starting draw.

**Plan for fuel.** DuroMax lists about 8 hours at half load on gasoline. Heavy loads burn far more, so a long outage means many cans or a 40 lb or larger propane tank. It weighs over 200 lb, so keep the path from the garage flat.

Owners report it starts reliably and carries big loads; the usual complaints are noise and weight. Before you buy, price a small standby like the [Guardian 14kW](/gear/generac-guardian-14kw/), and see where it ranks in our [home generator for power outages](/best-home-generator-for-power-outages/) guide.

faqs.q: Can the DuroMax XP12000EH run central air?
faqs.a: Sometimes. It offers 9,500 running watts on gasoline, and a 2- to 3-ton central AC typically runs at roughly 2,500 to 3,500 watts but can need several times that to start. A soft-start kit on the condenser makes it far more likely to work. Wire it through a 50-amp inlet and interlock, and keep other big motors off while the AC starts.

faqs.q: What is the difference between the XP12000EH and XP12000E?
faqs.a: The EH is dual fuel; the [XP12000E](/gear/duromax-xp12000e-gas/) runs on gasoline only. Both are rated at 9,500 running and 12,000 starting watts on gasoline from a 457cc engine, and both have a 50-amp outlet. The EH adds propane at 9,025 running watts, which lets you store fuel that does not go stale. Pick the E only if you will never use propane.

name: Westinghouse WGen9500
summary: A 9,500-watt gasoline portable with remote start and both 30-amp and 50-amp 240V outlets, for homes that need headroom past the 8,000-watt class.
verdict:
The WGen9500 gives you a step up from the 8,000-watt class without a big jump in tier, plus a key fob that starts it from the porch. Pick it when your load list sits between 7,000 and 9,000 watts.

**The headroom matters.** Westinghouse rates it at 9,500 running and 12,500 starting watts on gasoline from a 457cc engine. Compared with an 8,000-watt unit, the extra 1,500 running watts is enough for a window AC or a larger well pump on top of a fridge, freezer and furnace blower.

**Two 240V outlets.** The panel carries two 5-20R duplex outlets, a 30-amp [L14-30R](/glossary/l14-30/) and a 50-amp 14-50R. Use the L14-30 with a 30-amp [transfer switch](/glossary/transfer-switch/) kit, or the 14-50 with a 50-amp inlet and interlock. A 30-amp, 240V circuit tops out at 7,200 watts, so the 50-amp path is how you use all 9,500.

**Fuel and size.** The 6.6-gallon tank has a fuel gauge and is rated for up to 12 hours at 25% load; expect much less at heavy load. It is a big, heavy open-frame unit, so plan a level spot outside, well away from windows. Check whether the unit you buy is the newer version with a CO sensor.

Owners report easy remote starts and steady power; the common complaints are weight and fuel use at high load. It is in our [best gas generator](/best-gas-generator/) guide, next to the [Generac GP8000E](/gear/generac-gp8000e/).

faqs.a: Not a whole house with central air and electric appliances, but most essentials. At 9,500 running watts it can carry a fridge, freezer, well pump, furnace blower, lights and a window AC together if motors start one at a time. To use all of it, connect through the 50-amp 14-50R and a 50-amp inlet, since a 30-amp circuit caps out at 7,200 watts.

faqs.q: WGen9500 vs WGen9500DF: what is the difference?
faqs.a: The [WGen9500DF](/gear/westinghouse-wgen9500df/) adds propane. Both are rated at 9,500 running and 12,500 starting watts on gasoline, with a 6.6-gallon tank and both 30-amp and 50-amp outlets. On propane the DF makes 8,500 running watts. If you want fuel that stores for years without going stale, the DF is worth the small step up.

name: Firman P08004
summary: A budget 8,000-watt gasoline portable with remote start, an 8-gallon tank and a 50-amp outlet, for big essentials loads at a lower tier than the big brands.
verdict:
The P08004 is the budget route to 8,000-watt output. You give up some brand polish, but you keep the outlets and runtime that matter for home backup.

**Output and outlets.** Firman rates it at 8,000 running and 10,000 starting watts from a 439cc engine. The panel lists a 120V L5-30R, a 120/240V [L14-30R](/glossary/l14-30/) and a 120/240V 14-50R, so it can feed either a 30-amp transfer switch or a 50-amp inlet. Firman rates the 14-50R at 33.3 amps, which works out to the full 8,000 watts at 240 volts.

**Runtime is a strength.** The 8-gallon tank is larger than most rivals in this class, and Firman lists about 12 hours of run time. That means fewer refills overnight. Treat the [run time](/glossary/run-time/) figure as a best case at moderate load; heavy loads cut it sharply.

**Start options.** It has recoil, electric and remote start, which helps in bad weather. The listed noise is 74 dB, typical for an open-frame unit, so keep it at least 20 feet from the house with the exhaust pointing away.

Owners report good value and easy starts; the common complaints are noise and a heavy frame that takes two people to lift. Compare it with the [Generac GP8000E](/gear/generac-gp8000e/) in our [best gas generator](/best-gas-generator/) guide, and size your loads with the [wattage calculator](/tools/generator-wattage-calculator/).

faqs.q: Can the Firman P08004 run a well pump and fridge together?
faqs.a: Yes, in most cases. A 1 HP 240V submersible typically needs around 1,000 running watts and a fridge roughly 700, which leaves plenty of the 8,000 running watts for a freezer, furnace blower and lights. Start the pump first through a transfer switch, then the other motors, so the 10,000 starting watts are not shared by two motor starts at once.

faqs.q: Firman P08004 vs Generac GP8000E: which is better?
faqs.a: They are rated the same, 8,000 running and 10,000 starting watts. The Firman adds a 50-amp 14-50R, remote start and an 8-gallon tank, and sits in a lower price tier. The Generac adds COsense carbon monoxide shutoff and a wider service network. If automatic CO shutoff matters most, pick the Generac; for outlets and runtime per dollar, the Firman.

name: DuroMax XP12000E
summary: The gasoline-only version of the DuroMax 12,000-watt portable, with a 50-amp outlet for a large inlet, suited to buyers who are sure they will never run on propane.
verdict:
The XP12000E makes sense only if you are sure you will never want propane. It has the same gasoline output as the dual fuel [XP12000EH](/gear/duromax-xp12000eh/), minus the second fuel.

**Output.** DuroMax rates it at 9,500 running and 12,000 starting watts on gasoline from a 457cc engine with electric start. That is enough for a fridge, freezer, well pump, furnace blower and lights at once, with room for a window AC. A small central AC with a soft-start kit may also fit, depending on its starting draw.

**Use the 50-amp outlet.** It carries a 120/240V 50-amp outlet, so you can feed a 50-amp inlet such as the [Reliance PBN50](/gear/reliance-pbn50/) and a panel interlock. A 30-amp, 240V connection caps you at 7,200 watts, so the 50-amp path is the only way to use the full rating.

**Fuel math.** A big gasoline engine at heavy load empties its tank in hours, not days. Over a three-day outage that adds up to many cans of stabilized fuel, which is why the dual fuel version, or a standby on natural gas, often wins for long outages.

Owners report strong output for the money; the usual complaints are weight, noise and fuel burn. It appears in our [best gas generator](/best-gas-generator/) guide. Run your loads through the [wattage calculator](/tools/generator-wattage-calculator/) before you buy.

faqs.q: Can the DuroMax XP12000E power a whole house?
faqs.a: Most of a house with gas heat, yes, but not every load at once. Its 9,500 running watts cover the fridge, freezer, well pump, furnace blower, lights and a window AC. Central air, an electric range or an electric water heater will push past it. Feed it through a 50-amp inlet and interlock, and switch big loads on one at a time.

faqs.q: Is the XP12000E or XP12000EH the better buy?
faqs.a: The XP12000EH for most people. Both make 9,500 running and 12,000 starting watts on gasoline from a 457cc engine. The EH adds propane at 9,025 running watts, and propane stores for years without stabilizer. Choose the gasoline-only E only if you already keep fresh fuel rotated and never plan to use a propane tank.

name: DuroMax XP13000HXT Tri Fuel
summary: A tri fuel portable that runs on gasoline, propane or natural gas, rated 10,500 watts on gas, for homes with a gas line that want long outages without fuel runs.
verdict:
The XP13000HXT is the portable to buy if your house already has natural gas. Tri fuel means it can run from the gas line for as long as pressure holds, which removes the biggest problem with portables in a long outage.

**Three fuels, three ratings.** DuroMax's spec sheet lists 10,500 running and 13,000 peak watts on gasoline, 9,500 and 12,000 on propane, and 8,500 and 10,000 on natural gas, from a 500cc engine. Even the natural gas figure covers a fridge, freezer, well pump, furnace blower and lights with room left over.

**The gas hookup is the real cost.** You need a plumber to add a quick-connect and confirm your gas supply can feed the engine at the pressure DuroMax specifies. A long run of small pipe may not keep up. Budget for that work and for an inlet and [transfer switch](/glossary/transfer-switch/).

**Runtime and safety.** On gasoline, DuroMax lists 8.5 hours at half load; on propane, 6.5 hours. CO Alert shuts the engine down if carbon monoxide builds up, a backup to good placement, not a substitute. Our [CO shutoff](/glossary/co-shutoff/) entry explains what these sensors can and cannot do.

Owners report strong output and like the natural gas option; the common complaints are weight and noise. It appears in our [best dual fuel generator](/best-dual-fuel-generator/) guide. If you want hands-off operation on the same gas line, compare the [Champion 14kW aXis](/gear/champion-14kw-axis/).

faqs.q: Can the DuroMax XP13000HXT run on natural gas for days?
faqs.a: Yes, as long as gas pressure holds and you keep up with oil service. On natural gas it is rated at 8,500 running watts and 10,000 peak watts. Follow the manual's oil-change intervals during continuous use, and have a plumber confirm your supply meets DuroMax's pressure spec, since a weak supply cuts output and can stall motor starts.

faqs.q: XP13000HXT vs XP13000EH: what is the difference?
faqs.a: The HXT adds natural gas and CO Alert. Both are rated at 13,000 peak and 10,500 running watts on gasoline from a 500cc engine. The [XP13000EH](/gear/duromax-xp13000eh/) is dual fuel only, rated at 9,975 running watts on propane. If you have a gas line, the HXT running at 8,500 watts on natural gas means no fuel runs at all.

name: Generac Guardian 14kW
summary: The entry Guardian worth a whole-house look: 14kW on both propane and natural gas, for smaller homes or essential-circuit backup that starts itself.
verdict:
The Guardian 14kW is the entry point to automatic backup for smaller homes, or for larger ones that only need essentials. It is the best value in the Guardian line if your loads fit.

**Same rating on both fuels.** Generac rates it at 14,000 watts on propane and 14,000 watts on natural gas, unusual in a line where natural gas ratings usually drop. At 240 volts, 14,000 watts is about 58 amps, and Generac fits a 60-amp main breaker. That covers a fridge, freezer, furnace, well pump, lights and one smaller central AC, if the AC is the only big motor starting at once.

**Fuel use is modest.** Generac lists 1.81 gallons of propane per hour at half load and 195 cubic feet of natural gas per hour. A 500-gallon tank at 80% fill (400 gallons) is about 220 hours at half load, more than nine days.

**Install.** It uses the G-Force 800 engine and weighs 385 lb, so it needs a pad, a permit and licensed trades, plus an [automatic transfer switch](/glossary/transfer-switch/). Whole-house switches with load management help it carry homes that would otherwise need the [Guardian 18kW](/gear/generac-guardian-18kw/).

Owners report reliable starts and a smaller install footprint; the main complaint is that homes with two AC units outgrow it. See our [Generac generator cost](/generac-generator-cost/) guide for install budgets, and our [standby generator](/glossary/standby-generator/) entry for how these systems work.

name: Generac Guardian 18kW
summary: A mid-size Guardian rated 18kW on propane and 17kW on natural gas, for homes that outgrow the 14kW but do not need the full 22kW, central air included.
verdict:
The Guardian 18kW is the middle of Generac's air-cooled line, and for many mid-size homes it is the right size. It costs less to buy than the 22kW while still covering a central AC.

**Size it to your loads.** Generac rates it at 18,000 watts on propane and 17,000 watts on natural gas. At 240 volts, 17,000 watts is about 71 amps. A 3-ton central AC, fridge, freezer, furnace, well pump and lighting usually fit, with the AC as the largest single start. Run the [wattage calculator](/tools/generator-wattage-calculator/) if you also have an electric dryer or range.

**Fuel use.** Generac lists 1.70 gallons of propane per hour at half load and 3.02 at full load. A 500-gallon tank at 80% fill is about 235 hours at half load or 132 hours at full load. On natural gas it runs as long as utility pressure holds.

**Install.** It uses Generac's G-Force 800 engine and weighs 420 lb. You need a pad, a permit, a gas fitter, an electrician and an [automatic transfer switch](/glossary/transfer-switch/). Whole-house switch packages with load management let it handle homes with a second big load.

Owners report reliable automatic starts and like the Mobile Link app; the main complaint is that the step to the [Guardian 22kW](/gear/generac-guardian-22kw/) is small, so some wish they had sized up. Our [home generator for power outages](/best-home-generator-for-power-outages/) guide covers sizing in more depth.

name: Generac Guardian 24kW
summary: A larger air-cooled Guardian rated 24kW on propane and 21kW on natural gas, for bigger propane-fed homes with two AC units that want automatic backup.
verdict:
The Guardian 24kW is the step up for large homes where the 22kW is borderline. Buy it for propane-fed homes that want the extra 2,000 watts; on natural gas, the gain is small.

**Read the natural gas line.** Generac rates it at 24,000 watts on propane and 21,000 watts on natural gas. That natural gas figure matches what Generac's current page lists for the 22kW (older 22kW units were rated 19,500 watts), so on utility gas the two carry similar loads. At 240 volts, 24,000 watts is 100 amps on propane.

**What it can carry.** On propane, a 4-ton central AC, a second smaller AC, a fridge, freezer, well pump and lighting can fit together, especially with load management on the second AC. Check your list with the [wattage calculator](/tools/generator-wattage-calculator/).

**Fuel use.** Generac lists 2.53 gallons of propane per hour at half load and 3.9 at full load. A 500-gallon tank at 80% fill lasts about 158 hours at half load or about 103 hours at full load. It uses the 999cc G-Force 1000 engine and weighs 455 lb.

Owners report it handles big homes without load juggling; the common complaints are installation cost and propane use under heavy load. It pairs with an [automatic transfer switch](/glossary/transfer-switch/). See the [Guardian 26kW](/gear/generac-guardian-26kw/) for the next size up and our [Generac generator cost](/generac-generator-cost/) guide for install budgets.

faqs.q: Guardian 24kW vs 22kW: is the upgrade worth it?
faqs.a: On propane it buys 2,000 more watts, 24,000 versus 22,000, which is worth it if a load calculation puts you near the 22kW's limit. On natural gas, Generac's current pages list both at 21,000 watts, so the [22kW](/gear/generac-guardian-22kw/) usually makes more sense. Both use the 999cc G-Force 1000 engine and list 2.53 gal/hr of propane at half load.

name: Generac Guardian 26kW
summary: Generac's largest air-cooled Guardian, rated 26kW on propane and 22.5kW on natural gas, for large homes that want whole-house backup without a liquid-cooled unit.
verdict:
The Guardian 26kW is the most power you can get from Generac's air-cooled line. Choose it for large homes with two AC units or electric appliances before you look at liquid-cooled models.

**Size it to your loads.** Generac rates it at 26,000 watts on propane and 22,500 watts on natural gas, with a 110-amp main breaker. At 240 volts, 22,500 watts is about 94 amps. On natural gas that is 1,500 watts more than the 24kW, which makes it the better upgrade for gas-line homes.

**What it carries.** Two central AC units, a fridge, freezer, well pump, furnace and lighting can run together on propane with sensible start sequencing. An electric range or water heater may still call for load management. Check with the [wattage calculator](/tools/generator-wattage-calculator/).

**Fuel use.** Generac lists 2.06 gallons of propane per hour at half load and 3.63 at full load, and 333 cubic feet of natural gas per hour at full load. A 500-gallon tank at 80% fill lasts roughly 194 hours at half load or about 110 hours at full load. It uses the G-Force 1000 engine and weighs 518 lb.

Owners report it runs big homes without load juggling; the common complaint is install cost, which climbs with the larger wire and gas pipe a unit this size needs. It needs an [automatic transfer switch](/glossary/transfer-switch/) such as the [Generac RXSW200A3](/gear/generac-rxsw200a3/), and our [Generac generator cost](/generac-generator-cost/) guide covers what the install adds.

faqs.q: Is the Generac Guardian 26kW enough for a 4,000 square foot home?
faqs.a: Often, if heat is gas. Square footage matters less than loads: two central AC units, a well pump, fridges and lighting usually fit within 26,000 watts on propane or 22,500 on natural gas. All-electric homes with heat strips or electric water heaters may need load management. Ask your installer for a load calculation rather than sizing by square feet.

faqs.q: Guardian 26kW vs 24kW: what is the difference?
faqs.a: On propane, 2,000 watts: 26,000 versus 24,000. On natural gas the gap is 1,500 watts, 22,500 versus 21,000, which is the stronger reason to choose the 26kW on a gas line. The 26kW weighs 518 lb versus 455 lb and carries a 110-amp main breaker. Both use Generac's G-Force 1000 engine and need an automatic transfer switch.

name: Kohler 20RESCL
summary: Kohler’s 20kW air-cooled standby with a composite enclosure, rated 20kW on propane and 18kW on natural gas, the main alternative to a Generac Guardian 22kW.
verdict:
The Kohler 20RESCL is the standby to quote against a Generac Guardian 22kW. It gives up a little output and gains a lower listed sound level and a different dealer network.

**Output.** Kohler rates it at 20,000 watts on propane and 18,000 watts on natural gas, with the fuel set at install. At 240 volts, 18,000 watts is 75 amps. That covers a 3- to 4-ton central AC, fridge, freezer, furnace, well pump and lights in most homes. Compared with the [Guardian 22kW](/gear/generac-guardian-22kw/), you have 2,000 fewer watts on propane, so check your list with the [wattage calculator](/tools/generator-wattage-calculator/).

**Sound and build.** Listings give 64 dB(A) during its exercise run and 69 dB(A) under load, measured at 7 meters (23 feet). The 999cc Kohler CH1000 engine runs at 3,600 rpm, and the composite enclosure cannot rust.

**Fuel use.** Listings give 2.2 gallons of propane per hour at half load and 3.7 at full load, or 161 and 281 cubic feet of natural gas. A 500-gallon tank at 80% fill is about 180 hours at half load.

Owners report reliable starts and a solid enclosure; the most common complaint is that Kohler dealers are thinner on the ground than Generac's in some regions. It needs an [automatic transfer switch](/glossary/transfer-switch/). Compare it with the other standby picks in our [home generator for power outages](/best-home-generator-for-power-outages/) guide.

name: Champion 14kW aXis Home Standby (100515)
summary: Champion’s 14kW home standby, rated 14kW on propane and 12.5kW on natural gas, with a 62 dBA rating and a 10-year limited warranty, a value rival to the Guardian 14kW.
verdict:
The Champion 14kW aXis is the value alternative to the Generac Guardian 14kW. It brings a long warranty and a low rated noise level to the entry standby class.

**Output.** Champion rates it at 14,000 watts on propane and 12,500 watts on natural gas, with 120/240V single-phase output. At 240 volts, 12,500 watts is about 52 amps. That runs a fridge, freezer, furnace, well pump, lights and one smaller central AC if starts are staggered. On natural gas, the [Guardian 14kW](/gear/generac-guardian-14kw/) holds its full 14,000 watts, so it has the edge for gas-line homes.

**Quiet and warranty.** Champion lists 62 dBA, among the lowest figures in this class, and backs it with a 10-year limited warranty, twice the 5-year limited warranty on Generac's air-cooled units. The aXis controller has a 4-inch color display.

**A system, not a box.** The generator, model 100515, needs Champion's aXis automatic transfer switch for full function. Bundles pair it with 100-, 150- or 200-amp aXis switches (models 100835, 100836 and 100837). Plan on a pad, a permit, a gas fitter and an electrician, as with any [standby generator](/glossary/standby-generator/).

Owners report quiet operation and good value; the main complaint is a smaller installer network than Generac or Kohler. Size your loads with the [wattage calculator](/tools/generator-wattage-calculator/), and see how standby compares with portables in our [home generator for power outages](/best-home-generator-for-power-outages/) guide.

Champion sells bundles with 100-amp, 150-amp and 200-amp aXis switches, models 100835, 100836 and 100837. Buy the bundle sized to your service panel rather than mixing brands.

name: Generac GP6500
summary: A 6,500-watt gasoline portable with COsense CO shutoff and a 30-amp L14-30R outlet, sized for a fridge, freezer, sump pump and furnace through a transfer switch.
verdict:
The GP6500 is the right portable for a house that needs the essentials and a transfer switch, not a whole-home setup. It is smaller, lighter and easier on fuel than the 8,000-watt class.

**Size it to your loads.** Generac rates it at 6,500 running and 8,125 starting watts. A fridge (about 700 running watts), a freezer, a sump pump, a gas furnace blower, lights and internet total roughly 3,000 to 4,000 watts, leaving room to start one motor at a time. A 240V well pump up to about 1 HP is usually in reach. Check your list with the [wattage calculator](/tools/generator-wattage-calculator/).

**Runtime is a strength.** The 389cc engine pulls from a 7.9-gallon tank, and Generac's manual lists 11.5 hours at half load and 16.5 hours at quarter load. That gets you through a night without refueling.

**Outlets and safety.** The panel has two 20-amp GFCI duplex outlets and a 120/240V 30-amp [L14-30R](/glossary/l14-30/), the plug most manual switches use, such as the [Reliance 31406CRK](/gear/reliance-31406crk/). COsense shuts the engine down if carbon monoxide builds up. The recoil version weighs about 172 lb; the electric-start GP6500E is heavier.

Owners report easy starting and long runtime per tank; the common complaint is that it is loud next to an inverter generator. For more headroom, compare the [GP8000E](/gear/generac-gp8000e/) and the larger picks in our [best gas generator](/best-gas-generator/) guide.

faqs.q: Can the Generac GP6500 run a refrigerator and a sump pump?
faqs.a: Yes, easily. A typical fridge runs at about 700 watts and a 1/2 HP sump pump at roughly 1,000, both well inside 6,500 running watts. The 8,125 starting watts handle both motors, especially if they do not start at the same instant. That leaves room for a freezer, furnace blower, lights and Wi-Fi.

faqs.q: How long does the Generac GP6500 run on a tank?
faqs.a: Generac's manual lists 11.5 hours at half load and 16.5 hours at quarter load from the 7.9-gallon tank. Half load is about 3,250 watts, typical for a fridge, freezer, furnace and lights. Heavier loads shorten that. Keep stabilized gasoline on hand for a multi-day outage, and refuel only with the engine off and cool.
